Reviewer #2:

I looked forward to reading this paper. Senior author Franks is an emerging force in the systems neurophysiology of piriform cortex who has earned respect from his colleagues, including myself, for his independent work. Joint senior author Abbott is a computational neuroscientist of the first rank. Respect to the first authors as well for their acceptance into these mentors' labs; I will look forward to their future work. But this manuscript is not something that any of these authors will want on their conscience. It is a loosely-vetted and ultimately generic set of simulations based on substantial apparent ignorance of the underlying systems and of the value and limitations of computational modeling as a research strategy. It is likely to have value as a starting point for computational exploration of the system, but none of the present findings offer insight; they are simple, deterministic outcomes of the LIF circuit motifs used, with all of the interesting and mysterious features of piriform cortex explicitly omitted from the study.

The concrete goals of the model are unclear, but the title indicates that the central finding is a transformation from temporal to ensemble coding, referring here to an emphasis on sequences of activity in OB generating characteristic 'spatial' activity patterns across PCx pyramidal neurons. To do this, the authors built a randomly connected network between LIF neurons labeled MCs and another labeled PCx pyramidal cells, plus two classes of PCx interneurons. The MC-PCx mapping determines an ensemble-to-ensemble transformation, with the 'temporal' aspect contributing by spreading out MC activity in time so that only the earliest activated MCs constitute the relevant 'ensemble'. The suppression of PCx pyramidal responses by FBIs contributes to this temporal selectivity, as later-activating MCs have a much reduced field of excitable PCx neurons to activate. Probably this effect would be even stronger if PCx pyramidal activity was scored within the first volley rather than over the full 200 ms stimulation (including after the rebound from FBI inhibition), but that's a detail. This is fine so far – a simple implementation of well-known response properties in PCx that could be a foundation for interesting further development. But most of what the authors proceed to at this point is just to activate this simple LIF circuit motif in straightforward ways and claim, implausibly, that they have learned something about the piriform cortex.

For example, there is the issue of timescale. The olfactory bulb is one of the canonical oscillogenic circuits of the brain, generating endogenous γ rhythmicity from unpatterned (or theta-patterned input arising from respiration and/or ET cell dynamics) input. OB-PCx interactions are coordinated in the β band, which supersedes γ via a transitional mechanism that remains unclear. These γ/β frequencies are generally the frequencies considered relevant for spike phase coding effects, as received and transformed by postsynaptic integration and plasticity mechanisms such as STDP. On the order of ten different labs over the years have dedicated substantial effort to measuring, analyzing, and understanding these fast OB (and to a lesser extent PCx) dynamics, both physiologically and in a coding sense. Many more groups pursue analogous neuronal systems dynamics questions in other structures, particularly hippocampus. Yet, in recent years, a corner of the olfaction literature has arisen that seems to not understand this body of work, or the relevance of the dynamical systems that underlie it, and has instead borrowed key concepts and catchphrases from this body of work and applied them naively to respiratory theta "oscillations". The deployment of citations in the introduction to this paper suggests that the authors are among those who do not understand this distinction, or appreciate its importance. For a dynamically-based model to simply omit mention of the central dynamics of this system is disqualifying. It renders the essential premise being tested in this paper incorrect and the outcome of the associated model all but irrelevant. This would be a critical problem even if the rest of the authors' approach was defensible.

This criticism may sound strange, because the Introduction is full of citations that, if skimmed, might appear to loosely support the premise constructed if one knew nothing of the literature omitted. But upon closer and more critical reading, the constructed premise does not stand. For example, some references note phenomenological responses as a side point to the chief goals of the corresponding paper. This manuscript uncritically interprets such reports as broadly vetted truths that will withstand the vagaries of sensory sampling in natural environments, even when a rudimentary understanding of physiological principles would make the error clear. Sometimes the reference in question bears responsibility for the error by overgeneralizing their findings or indulging a favorite hypothesis. Sometimes not. But the naïve rank-based temporal sequence hypotheses on the theta timescale for odor coding don't pass the sniff test. Response replicability under tightly controlled conditions is a deterministic near-tautology; it does not suffice to defend a hypothesis of coding. The entire central problem of olfaction is signal identification in the presence of copious and usually unpredictable noise; we know that virtually no easily-recognizable aspect of the signal is replicable in competing backgrounds, or in awake, behaving animals.

But if we ignore the timescale issue and accept the hypothesis of spike rank coding on a respiratory timescale (for sake of argument), along with the convergence and divergence of MC->Pyr connectivity, what will this offer us? The interesting features of PCx are its intrinsic dynamics, its emergent shared dynamics with OB, its hypothesized pattern-completion capabilities, and the idea that it may be a primary location for the integration of afferent odor input with existing odor memories. However, all of these are explicitly excluded from consideration by the present authors. This is problematic, because any one of these features, if implemented, would substantially dominate the core response properties of the piriform cortex to afferent input. Omitting all of them essentially predetermines that the outcome of the simulation will be irrelevant to any application. Constructing the model explicitly from LIF neurons further rules out the possibility of finding interesting biophysical mechanisms underlying PCx response properties.

But if we set these difficult problems aside, knowing that simulations also can serve as test beds for emergent circuit properties that may help us understand these more complex hypothesized functions, then what questions can the remaining model help us address? The authors answer (1) explaining spatially distributed ensemble codes for odor identity, (2) normalization across odor concentrations, and (3) the revelation of temporal codes for odor intensity.

Spatially distributed ensemble codes have been shown experimentally, of course. In the present model, the transform is essentially predetermined… different odors are defined by their different profiles of activation across glomeruli, and latencies of each. The divergence/convergence pattern onto PCx generate odor-specific patterns among PCx neurons: a generic spatial transform. This isn't a finding; it has been a foundational principle for decades. The selectivity for early MC responses is an idea, presumably motivated by rapid behavioral responses and fast functional adaptation in PCx pyramidal cells. I suppose hypothesizing that FBI feedback is primarily responsible for PCx pyramidal neuron response adaptation is potentially of interest, but this would need to be developed further.

"Thus, while our simplified PCx-like model does recapitulate the overall pattern of odor ensembles across PCx, ways in which it fails to do so makes specific predictions about cortical connectivity." This statement is fundamentally untrue. The model doesn't match the data, and the authors have some vague ideas about model limitations vis a vis reality that might bear on the difference. These aren't "specific predictions", especially because no effort at all is made to explore them. I'm not going to repeat myself more, but most of the conclusions within Results paragraphs are of this nature – the sort of throwaway interpretive comments that often fill the tail ends of Discussion sections. The value of modeling is to quantify and/or challenge hypotheses that are not simple enough to be otherwise obvious. Modeling results deserve and require the same critical assessment as experimental results – do they really mean what they seem to, or are there extraneous variables that dominate the outcome? Are we predetermining the outcome by the way in which we set up the experiment, bypassing the actual question of interest? This is really important to understand if one wants to be a consequential theoretical neuroscientist.

Normalization across odor concentrations. In sensory systems, it's just not reasonable to insert the main afferent intensity tolerance circuitry after the second synapse. Indeed, the authors acknowledge that most of this takes place earlier, substantially in the OB glomerular layer. But of course cortical circuits (almost?) all regulate local circuit input intensities, presumably because of the narrow dynamic ranges of neurons and the often narrower ranges of functional circuits. So it's not strictly wrong to refer to FFI and FBI in the PCx circuit as concentration normalization, but I would call it misleading. If you have negative feedback, then you have a capability that you could call 'intensity normalization' if you set up an experiment to show you that and had narrative reasons to call it that. But this is really different from a claim of "concentration normalization" in a chemosensory system.

But, setting that aside, what do we learn from the present model? The authors favor FBI as the main normalizing force, which is fine. But this isn't really a finding. First, 'normalization' implies FBI, as you can't truly normalize without feedback. However, nominal FFI circuits often embed feedback effects, as do those in the present model in which broad MC->FFI projections and FFI-FFI interconnectivity are likely to produce some sort of global quasi-average activity level among FF interneurons for delivery onto PCx pyramidal cells that can serve as quasi-normalization so long as the gains are roughly matched. But more to the point, to conclude that FBI is the dominant effect requires exploration of the parameter spaces. Under what circumstances is this so? What if FBI were weaker, and FFI stronger? What if FFI were sigmoidal in effect and very strong, so that it reliably constrains PCx activation within a narrow range? How about some assessment of the innate requirement for both, because tuned FFI ensures that the pyramidal cells can respond within their dynamic ranges whereas FBI can further tune Pyr cell activity (surely for more interesting purposes that fine-tuning concentration normalization, though). The interpretation (finding?) that FFI is subtractive is particularly baffling – of course it is so in the model, because the authors' LIF inhibitory synapses are subtractive. The GABA(A) synapses in the actual PCx will be predominantly divisive. It's a bug, not a feature.

The revelation of temporal codes for odor intensity I can't speak to. The effects emerge from a model that is missing most of the important features that would affect this finding, and that is not challenged by odor competition, correlated noise, or difficult discriminations. In the present model, this finding is an unavoidable consequence of the deterministic system and the particular models used for concentration (whether altering the number of glomeruli activated or stretching/compressing their activation in time). The model isn't constrained by olfactory physiology anywhere near well enough to generalize this effect to the real system.

Overall, this model is a generic spatial-to-spatial transformation circuit model with a temporal selectivity element added on. It is loosely based on the synaptology of piriform cortex (in the sense that it lumps several classes of neurons into larger groups) but dominated by standard FF and FB circuit motifs. Few surprises are possible because of the simple LIF models and straightforward connectivity maps. Diversity in cell types, biophysical properties, and the main interesting features of piriform cortex are omitted by design. So what is the point of the model? Just to reshape the odor representation again into a new form? We know that already, both from PCx data and from what randomly connected layers of LIF neurons do. What is the utility of this transformation?

The experiments associated with Figure 3 have the most potential; they start engaging with the dynamics of PCx circuitry. But there is a lot to do to actually assess the potential roles of these different interneuron classes, as opposed to generating a just-so story.

I want to be supportive of this work; I genuinely do. But to be supportive of the authors, which is ultimately more important, I instead offer this fairly harsh review. I'm sorry for that, but it is necessary.

results.result: Experimental recordings from awake mice show that OB outputs are sustained throughout the sniff cycle while PCx responses are sparse and transient, peaking shortly after inhalation. This supports the transformation from a temporal code in OB to an ensemble code in PCx where early-active glomeruli preferentially define cortical responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C33 provide direct experimental evidence from simultaneous OB and PCx recordings (Figure 1) showing distinct temporal dynamics. Claims C34-C35 appropriately synthesize these observations with cited literature to conclude that early OB inputs preferentially shape PCx ensembles. The experimental data directly support this interpretation.

results.result: The authors developed a computational model of the OB-PCx circuit with 900 glomeruli (each with 25 mitral cells) providing input to 10,000 pyramidal cells, 1225 FFINs, and 1225 FBINs, with connectivity patterns approximating known anatomy.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 describe the model architecture in detail. The model structure is clearly specified with biologically-constrained parameters. While the model is simplified (e.g., single MTC population, random connectivity), the authors acknowledge these limitations and justify design choices based on experimental constraints.

results.result: The model produces spontaneous activity levels (2.8±0.4% of cells active) and odor-evoked responses (14.1±0.59% active at reference concentration) consistent with experimental observations, though trial-to-trial correlations are lower than experimentally measured.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 show the model recapitulates key experimental features with quantitative comparisons to literature. Claims C53-C55 acknowledge that correlation values are lower than experimental measurements and provide plausible explanations (gap junctions, broadly activated cells). The discrepancy is appropriately discussed rather than ignored.

results.result: The model shows that early-activated glomeruli initiate a cascade where pyramidal cells receiving strong OB input spike first, recurrent excitation recruits additional pyramidal cells with moderate input, and FBINs are then recruited to truncate the response while maintaining odor-specificity.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C67 describe the core mechanistic findings from the model (Figure 4). The cascade dynamics are well-characterized with clear temporal progression. The mechanism is internally consistent: early inputs drive initial spiking, recurrent excitation amplifies but remains subthreshold alone, and stronger FBIN recruitment prevents runaway excitation while preserving selectivity.

results.result: Removing recurrent circuitry from the model eliminates the transient peak response and causes pyramidal cell spiking to increase continuously throughout the sniff. Adding only FFI to the feedforward circuit does not restore the characteristic response dynamics.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C72 describe systematic circuit manipulations (Figure 4C, Figure 5—supplement 1A) demonstrating that intracortical circuitry is necessary for key response features. The comparison between full and reduced circuits clearly establishes that FFI alone cannot account for temporal selectivity, supporting the importance of recurrent dynamics.

results.result: FFI primarily controls the amplitude of the peak response in a subtractive manner, while pyramidal cell output is robust to FBI strength over a wide range, though extreme values cause runaway excitation or oscillations.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 describe systematic parameter variations (Figure 5) showing distinct roles for FFI and FBI. The robustness analysis is thorough, examining both inhibitory mechanisms across parameter ranges. The finding that FFI is subtractive while FBI provides divisive normalization is well-supported by the modeling results.

results.result: Recurrent excitation is responsible for both early amplification and rapid truncation of the population response. Increasing recurrent excitation onto pyramidal cells enhances the upward slope to the peak, while increasing excitation onto FBINs modulates the downward slope.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C84 describe systematic manipulation of recurrent excitation (Figure 6) with clear dissociation of effects on pyramidal cells versus FBINs. The bidirectional role of recurrent excitation (amplification and truncation) is well-demonstrated through parameter variations showing opposite effects on response dynamics.

results.result: In the full model, population spiking peaks at 34±8.3 ms when only ~15% of glomeruli have been activated. Eliminating FFI shifts the peak slightly earlier (28±4.5 ms), while removing recurrent excitation delays it substantially (139±29 ms), demonstrating that recurrent excitation amplifies early inputs and discounts later inputs.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 provide quantitative analysis (Figure 7) directly linking response timing to glomerular activation. The comparison across circuit manipulations clearly demonstrates the role of recurrent excitation in temporal selectivity. The statistics are appropriately reported with standard deviations.

results.result: Response correlations for same-odor trials are lower when using only the first 50 ms (0.24±0.019) versus full 200 ms (0.35±0.010), but the signal-to-noise ratio (same/different odor correlations) nearly doubles for early responses, indicating that early cortical activity provides a more distinctive odor representation.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C94 provide quantitative analysis (Figure 7E-F) showing that early responses have better discriminability despite lower absolute correlations. The signal-to-noise ratio calculation appropriately captures the trade-off between correlation magnitude and selectivity. This supports the functional importance of early temporal filtering.

results.result: The model shows concentration normalization: a 10-fold increase in active glomeruli (3% to 30%) produces only an 80% increase in responsive pyramidal cells (9.7±0.40% to 17.3±0.71%), with modest increases in total spikes and spikes per cell, consistent with experimental observations.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C99 demonstrate concentration invariance in the model (Figure 8B-E) with quantitative comparisons to experimental data. The normalization is substantial (10-fold input → 1.8-fold output) and matches experimental observations. The statistics are appropriately reported with standard deviations.

results.result: Eliminating FFI produces modest, uniform increases in responses across concentrations (subtractive effect), while removing recurrent excitation and FBI causes steep concentration-dependence (divisive effect). Recurrent excitation also amplifies responses at low concentrations, demonstrating bidirectional normalization.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C104 systematically dissect normalization mechanisms (Figure 8C-D) through circuit manipulations. The distinction between subtractive (FFI) and divisive (recurrent/FBI) normalization is clearly demonstrated. The bidirectional normalization (amplification at low input, suppression at high input) is a key mechanistic insight well-supported by the data.

results.result: A linear classifier trained at one concentration can accurately identify odors across concentrations when using only the first 50 ms of activity, but performance degrades at extreme concentrations when using full 200 ms responses. Early responses maintain better separation between same and different odor correlations across concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C111 demonstrate concentration-invariant odor recognition using decoding analysis (Figure 9A-B). The comparison between early (50 ms) and full (200 ms) responses clearly shows superior generalization for early activity. The mechanistic explanation (corruption by spontaneous activity at low concentrations, contamination by late inputs at high concentrations) is plausible.

results.result: Population synchrony is highly sensitive to concentration: a 10-fold increase in active glomeruli produces a 5.7-fold increase in peak spike rate but only 1.8-fold increase in responsive cells. Peak rate and latency can be used to decode concentration, with combined features performing best, though timing variability increases at high concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 demonstrate multiplexed coding where concentration is encoded in temporal features (Figure 9C-F). The quantitative analysis shows population synchrony is more sensitive to concentration than ensemble size. Multiple decoding approaches are tested, with appropriate acknowledgment of performance trade-offs across concentration ranges.

results.result: The model demonstrates how PCx circuitry implements a multiplexed odor code where recurrent excitation amplifies early OB inputs and recruits feedback inhibition to suppress later inputs, producing concentration-robust ensemble representations of odor identity while encoding concentration through population synchrony.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C6, C119-C121, C140-C141 synthesize the main findings into a coherent mechanistic framework. The multiplexed coding strategy (ensemble for identity, temporal for intensity) is well-supported by the modeling results. The circuit mechanism (recurrent amplification + feedback suppression) is clearly demonstrated through systematic manipulations.

results.result: The model suggests that circuit motif (feedforward vs. feedback) determines functional role more than cell type, with recurrent excitation/FBI providing divisive gain control while FFI provides subtractive modulation. This motif may be particularly suited for normalizing temporal or latency-based codes.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C126 draw broader conclusions about circuit organization from the modeling results. The distinction between circuit motif and cell type is well-supported by the differential effects of FFI versus FBI despite similar implementation. The speculation about applicability to other temporal codes (C126) is appropriately qualified.

results.result: The model makes several testable predictions: selective FFI blockade should produce additive increases without altering dynamics; FBI blockade should have multiplicative effects; reducing pyramidal output should increase and prolong responses and make them concentration-dependent; Connexin-36 knockout should increase trial-to-trial variability.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C132 derive specific experimental predictions from the model. These predictions follow logically from the mechanistic insights and are appropriately qualified as predictions rather than established facts. The predictions are testable with current experimental techniques (optogenetics, genetic knockouts).

results.result: The model does not recapitulate the biphasic PCx response observed experimentally, possibly because it does not distinguish mitral versus tufted cells or include centrifugal feedback from PCx to OB.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C135 acknowledge a specific limitation of the model with plausible explanations. The authors appropriately identify what the model fails to capture and provide mechanistic hypotheses for the discrepancy. This transparent discussion of limitations strengthens rather than weakens the overall work.

results.result: The model's focus on single-sniff responses is justified because trained rodents can discriminate odors within ~100 ms (one sniff), and early activity provides better concentration-invariant recognition because full responses are corrupted by spontaneous activity at low concentrations and late-responding glomeruli at high concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C139 justify the single-sniff modeling approach with behavioral evidence and provide mechanistic explanation for why early responses support better odor recognition. The justification is reasonable given the experimental literature, though the model cannot address multi-sniff dynamics or learning.

results.result: Prior work establishes that OB uses a temporal latency code for odor identity while PCx uses an ensemble code without additional spike timing information, representing a transformation from temporal to ensemble coding.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C7-C8, C19, C23-C24 accurately summarize the experimental literature on OB and PCx coding strategies. The citations are appropriate and the characterization of the transformation problem is consistent with current understanding. This provides the scientific context motivating the modeling work.

results.result: The model shows that only a small subset of PCx neurons need to receive suprathreshold OB input, with recurrent excitation recruiting additional cells that receive moderate but subthreshold input.
results.evaluation: Claim C122 is directly supported by the model dynamics shown in Figure 4B where cells receiving strong, moderate, and weak OB input show distinct recruitment patterns. This reconciles the sparse OB-to-PCx connectivity with the broader ensemble activation observed experimentally.

results.result: The authors propose that the OB-to-PCx transformation represents a more general circuit motif for interpreting temporally structured input, noting that recurrent normalization is effective in other systems using phasic or time-varying input.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C143 propose broader applicability of the circuit mechanism beyond olfaction. While C142 cites evidence from other systems, C143 is speculative. The proposal is reasonable but would require additional modeling or experimental work in other systems to validate. The speculation is appropriately qualified.

results.result: The model simulates concentration changes by scaling glomerular onset latencies while preserving activation sequences.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 describes the modeling approach for concentration, which is clearly implemented and justified by experimental observations (C95) showing that latencies decrease with concentration. This approach is reasonable though simplified, as it assumes perfect preservation of rank order across concentrations.
